speaker: Alex Schultz
title: Meta CMO: How Advertising Works Under the Hood
question: How should leaders evaluate whether AI adoption will ultimately shrink or grow total headcount at large tech companies?
guest: This comes back to three different things we talk about a lot internally. Thing number one is doing existing stuff more efficiently. Existing stuff is going to be done more efficiently with AI as it exists today without more breakthroughs—a lot of stuff can be automated, so there will be less of that work. Thing number two is things that literally weren't possible before will become possible, which can open up a lot more jobs—like semantic understanding of content for ranking short-form video and unconnected content, which could not exist without these models. Thing number three is things that were possible but prohibitively expensive suddenly cross the threshold of being reasonable and ROI-positive to do—like support chatbots, where you could do it with human beings before, it was just prohibitively expensive, and now AI does far better than a phone tree. Jobs will definitely go down in category one. How many jobs category two and category three create will determine whether some of these companies actually get bigger, because so many things are now ROI-positive to do.

points.core: Automating existing workflows with AI definitely reduces headcount in efficiency-driven roles.
points.note: Accept: doing current work more efficiently shrinks jobs in that category even without further AI breakthroughs. Do not credit: claiming AI will not eliminate any existing jobs.

points.core: AI unlocks previously impossible product capabilities that create entirely new areas of work.
points.note: Accept: capabilities that could not exist before modern AI, such as semantic content ranking for unconnected feeds, generating new teams or roles. Do not credit: generic 'new jobs will appear' platitudes without the previously-impossible category.

points.core: Tasks once prohibitively expensive to staff manually become ROI-positive with AI assistance.
points.note: Accept: previously feasible but uneconomical workloads—like human-escalated customer support at massive scale—crossing the ROI threshold to justify new staffing. Do not credit: conflating this with simple cost-cutting of already-staffed teams.

points.core: Net company headcount depends on whether newly unlocked work outweighs efficiency-driven job losses.
points.note: Accept: companies could even grow larger if job creation from newly possible and newly ROI-positive work exceeds automation reductions. Do not credit: flatly asserting headcount will definitely shrink or definitely grow without weighing the opposing buckets.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
Leaders should treat this as an empirical question about demand, not a foregone conclusion about technology. The key variable is elasticity: when AI makes work cheaper, does the company do more of it, or the same amount with fewer people? Software has historically shown elastic demand, since cheaper development led to more projects rather than fewer engineers, but that pattern is not guaranteed to hold.

Four things are worth evaluating. First, the backlog: if valuable work goes unbuilt because of capacity limits, productivity gains will likely be reinvested rather than cut. Second, task-level exposure: map which roles AI substitutes for (routine support, some coding and QA) versus complements (judgment, design, customer relationships). Third, the growth outlook: firms in expanding markets absorb productivity into growth, while mature or margin-pressured ones convert it into reductions. Fourth, new work created: AI infrastructure, evaluation, governance, and oversight roles.

Be skeptical of headlines too. Many layoffs attributed to AI reflect over-hiring corrections, interest rates, or capital shifting to AI spending.

Practically, track revenue per employee, measured productivity from pilots, and hiring mix over time, and plan for scenarios rather than a single forecast.

points.why: The response identifies tasks AI can substitute for but treats job reductions as conditional even in efficiency-driven roles.
The response lists AI-related roles without connecting them to product capabilities that were previously impossible.
The response discusses clearing capacity-constrained backlogs without showing that AI makes previously feasible but prohibitively expensive work ROI-positive.
The response weighs doing more work against doing the same work with fewer people, but never asks whether jobs created by newly unlocked work outnumber jobs lost to automation.

models.label: Gemini Carbon
models.answer: Leaders should evaluate headcount impact by weighing task substitution against demand elasticity, shifting organizational bottlenecks, and capital-allocation strategy. First, they must test whether AI-driven efficiency meets saturated or elastic demand: if cheaper, faster engineering merely delivers a fixed roadmap with fewer people, headcount shrinks; if lower build costs unlock previously uneconomical products, custom solutions, and markets, total labor demand can grow. Second, leaders should track where bottlenecks migrate. When routine coding and operations accelerate, constraints often shift toward system architecture, verification, security, product judgment, and go-to-market execution, reshaping the role mix rather than simply cutting staff. Third, competitive dynamics and capital choices are decisive: firms harvesting productivity gains to expand margins will trim teams, whereas companies forced by rivals to reinvest savings into new AI-native bets may hire aggressively. Practically, executives should look past isolated task-speedup metrics and watch two leading indicators: whether viable, high-return product backlogs are depleting or multiplying, and whether AI raises the marginal revenue produced by an additional augmented employee above their cost.

points.why: The response makes staffing cuts conditional on a fixed roadmap or a decision to expand margins, leaving the reduction in efficiency-driven roles unestablished.
The reference to AI-native bets does not identify any product capability that was previously impossible.
The response connects lower build costs to making previously uneconomical work viable and increasing labor demand.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer: Leaders should treat headcount as the result of competing forces rather than a fixed number of tasks waiting to be automated. The first question is demand elasticity. If AI makes engineering or support work cheaper, does the company's backlog of profitable work expand (the Jevons effect, which points to growth), or is demand roughly fixed (which points to shrinkage)? The second is task versus job exposure. AI usually automates parts of roles, so they should map which tasks get absorbed and whether what remains makes up a full job. Third, they should watch where capital goes. Heavy spending on compute and data centers often competes with payroll in the budget, so tight margins can cut jobs even when productivity gains are modest. Fourth, they should look for new work that AI itself creates, such as evaluation, safety, infrastructure, integration and new products. Finally, they should be skeptical of announcements. Many layoffs credited to AI really reflect over-hiring during the pandemic or pressure from interest rates. The most reliable signals come from their own pilots: measured output per worker, changes in hiring rates for entry-level roles, and whether teams that got productivity gains took on more scope or lost staff.

points.why: The response says AI automates parts of roles and treats the resulting job losses as conditional.
The response lists new roles and products without identifying capabilities that were impossible before AI.
The response asks whether cheaper work expands the profitable backlog without establishing that previously feasible but prohibitively expensive work becomes worth staffing.
The response explicitly weighs growth from expanded profitable work and AI-created work against shrinkage from efficiency gains when demand is fixed.

models.label: Gemini Neon
models.answer:
Leaders should evaluate AI's net headcount impact by balancing direct labor substitution against demand elasticity and reinvestment choices, rather than extrapolating from short-term efficiency gains alone. The central question is whether lower production costs unlock enough new demand—a Jevons paradox effect—to justify hiring into new products, markets, and faster release cycles, or whether core markets are mature enough that productivity gains simply reduce staffing needs.

To judge this, executives should map where AI automates routine tasks versus where it shifts bottlenecks toward human-intensive work like system architecture, product judgment, enterprise sales, and governance. They must also examine capital allocation and competitive pressure: companies focused on margin expansion will likely shrink headcount, while those competing aggressively for new AI-enabled revenue may grow or rapidly reshape their workforce. Tracking leading indicators—such as backlog growth, customer acquisition velocity, and where human oversight becomes the new constraint—provides a far more reliable signal than task-level automation estimates alone.

points.why: The response acknowledges labor substitution but presents staffing reductions as conditional on market maturity or margin strategy.
The response mentions new AI-enabled products and revenue without identifying capabilities that were previously impossible.
The response links lower costs to new demand but does not identify previously feasible workloads that become economical enough to justify staffing.
The response makes the net headcount outcome depend on whether hiring for newly unlocked work outweighs staffing reductions from automation.
quotes: balancing direct labor substitution against demand elasticity and reinvestment choices
whether lower production costs unlock enough new demand—a Jevons paradox effect—to justify hiring into new products, markets, and faster release cycles

models.label: GPT-6.2-Sol
models.answer:
Leaders should ask whether AI will expand the amount of work the company can profitably do faster than it reduces the labor needed for each unit of work. If demand is limited and AI removes enough work to consolidate roles, headcount may shrink. If lower costs or faster delivery unlock new products, customers, or projects, headcount can grow even as each team becomes more productive.

Build a forecast by business line against a credible baseline without AI. Use pilots to measure how much labor it takes to deliver the same output at the same quality, including review, rework, and oversight. Then estimate how much demand will grow, where bottlenecks will move, and which teams will need to hire. Track both near-term and multiyear effects, and include contractors so outsourcing doesn’t look like a reduction in labor. The most telling evidence is what happens to the capacity AI frees up. Is it absorbed through attrition, redeployed to existing work, or used to build businesses that need more people?

points.why: The response describes role consolidation as conditional and never commits to job losses in the existing workflows AI makes more efficient.
The response mentions new products and projects without identifying capabilities that were impossible before AI.
The response says lower costs can unlock work but leaves unclear whether that work was previously feasible and too expensive to staff.
The response explicitly weighs growth in profitable work against labor savings and explains how the company can grow despite higher productivity.
quotes: Leaders should ask whether AI will expand the amount of work the company can profitably do faster than it reduces the labor needed for each unit of work.
If lower costs or faster delivery unlock new products, customers, or projects, headcount can grow even as each team becomes more productive.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Astra
models.answer:
Leaders should compare two forecasts over the same time horizon: how many employees the company would need with AI and how many it would need without it. Headcount can rise after adoption even if AI slows hiring, so a before-and-after comparison can mislead.

Start with hours saved on specific tasks, then test whether those savings actually change staffing needs at the required quality level. Faster coding, for example, may do little for overall output if product review is the bottleneck. On the growth side, estimate how much additional demand lower prices or better products could generate, and how many people it would take to serve that demand and maintain the AI systems.

Model the near term and the longer term separately. Track output per employee, customer demand, hiring, and attrition against both forecasts. The decisive question is whether additional work creates enough demand for labor to outweigh the staffing needs AI removes.

The response links lower prices to higher demand without explaining how AI makes previously uneconomical workloads worth undertaking.
The response explicitly makes AI’s net headcount effect depend on whether additional work creates more jobs than AI removes.
